screens.title: Understanding Core Requirements and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Before designing any system, we must stop and understand what the system must do and how it must behave. In this chapter you will learn how to list functional requirements, translate quality needs into non-functional requirements, and produce initial capacity estimates that feed architecture choices. We study two small but instructive systems: a URL Shortener, which converts long links into short ones and must redirect extremely quickly, and a Pastebin, which stores text snippets for retrieval. You will see concrete use cases for creating, retrieving and managing content, and learn why redirects are read-heavy while pastes can be more balanced. We will also cover common trade-offs: availability vs consistency, latency vs cost, and durability strategies for stored content. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write clear requirement statements, perform QPS and storage calculations using the supplied assumptions, and identify the top operational risks to plan for. Think of this chapter as the foundation: if requirements and capacity are wrong, every later architectural decision becomes brittle. As you move forward, ask yourself which NFRs matter most to your users and how that changes storage, caching, and replication choices.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Understanding Requirements
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Understanding Core Requirements and Use Cases

We will identify functional vs non-functional needs, map primary user interactions for a URL Shortener and Pastebin, and produce capacity estimates that guide architecture.

16:9 HD Classroom
Why it matters
Good requirements prevent costly rework and drive correct choices for caching, storage, and replication.
What you will deliver
A prioritized requirement list, QPS/storage estimates, and a clear set of trade-offs to validate with stakeholders.
In this lesson
  • Define functional and non-functional requirements for both systems
  • Estimate writes, reads, and storage using the provided assumptions
  • Identify primary use cases, risks, and early trade-offs
Tip: Treat redirection latency and storage durability as separate design drivers.
Concept Snapshot
Foundations
Functional vs NFRs
What the system does versus how well it does it.
Capacity estimates
WPS, RPS and long-term storage shape choices like caching and replication.
Explore Key Topics
Requirements
List must-have functions and quality attributes before choosing technology.
Capacity
Quick calculations for WPS/RPS/storage guide scaling and cost trade-offs.
Trade-offs
Decide which NFRs to prioritize and accept practical compromises.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives slide, we set clear, testable skills you should gain. Objective one asks you to identify and separate functional requirements from non-functional requirements for both a URL Shortener and a Pastebin. You will learn to write concise functional statements like "shorten a given URL" or "create a new paste", and then pair each with the relevant quality constraints such as latency, availability, or security. Objective two focuses on capacity estimation: you will practice turning monthly or yearly volumes into writes per second, reads per second, and storage needs using the chapter's assumptions. This is not arithmetic practice alone — it's the habit of converting user stories into infrastructure requirements. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic that helps you remember whether an item is a function or a quality attribute, and a milestone marker you can use to verify competency. By practicing these objectives you will avoid a common mistake: designing systems before quantifying load and quality targets.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on applying and validating the skills you practiced earlier. You will practice calculating peaks and buffers: for example, rounding average writes and reads up to account for bursts and growth. The goal is to learn to design with a safety margin — we recommend planning for two to five times expected average RPS for peak capacity. You will also learn to reason about storage growth over years, not just months, and how that affects backup and retention choices. Finally, you will learn to translate user stories into acceptance criteria: e. g., a newly created short URL must redirect within a second, or a paste must be retrievable immediately after creation. Each card contains a mnemonic and a small micro-check you can use to confirm you have achieved the milestone. These are practical skills you will use in interview scenarios and real designs, where assumptions must be explained and justified.

screens.title: Functional Requirements: URL Shortener
screens.narratorSegment: A functional requirement states what the system must do. For a URL Shortener the core must-have functions are simple and specific: first, shorten a given URL — accept a long URL and return a unique short code or short URL; second, redirect a short URL to the original long URL. Those two requirements drive the A P I surface and the minimum data model: a short code, the original URL, creation metadata, and optional expiration or owner fields. Optional functional features often asked for in interviews include custom short codes, URL expiration rules, analytics for click counts and referrers, and user accounts for management. Each optional function adds complexity: custom codes require collision checks and namespaces, expirations add lifecycle management and cleanup jobs, and analytics need event collection and aggregation. A common misconception is to treat analytics as a core requirement; in many designs it can be implemented asynchronously to avoid slowing redirects. As a takeaway, write each function as a one-line statement and annotate whether it must be synchronous, can be eventual, or is optional. That clarity helps later decisions about consistency and performance.

keyIdea.text: Shorten and redirect are the mandatory functions; optional features like custom codes and analytics add complexity that should be justified.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Functional Requirements
Definition

What a URL Shortener must do

1
Shorten a given URL
Accept a long URL, generate or accept a short code, and return the short URL immediately.
2
Redirect short URL to original
Given a short code, perform an HTTP redirect to the stored original URL with very low latency.
Optional features include custom short codes, URL expiration, analytics, and user accounts; treat these as separate, prioritized requirements.
Key Takeaway

Write functions as single-line requirements and mark optional features as asynchronous when possible to keep redirects fast.

Example & Notes
Concrete example: when a user submits a long URL, the server should return a short code in the same API response. For immediate availability, the short code must be committed before responding. Analytics collection, however, can be recorded asynchronously to avoid slowing the API.
Misconception
Analytics must be synchronous. In practice, asynchronous event logging avoids making redirects slow or fragile.
Pro tip
Make the shorten API idempotent for retries by detecting duplicate long URLs or client-provided idempotency keys.
Why it matters: small, well-scoped functional requirements keep the design focused on the real user flows and avoid premature optimization.

screens.title: URL Shortener Use Cases and Flows
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the user flows makes it easy to convert requirements into APIs and operations. The primary flow for a URL Shortener has three steps: client submits a long URL, the system returns a short URL or code, and later a client requests the short URL which triggers a redirect to the original. Optional flows add steps: a user may request a custom code which requires collision checks, or set an expiration that schedules deletion. Analytics introduces a write-heavy event pipeline: each redirect can emit a click event with metadata for later aggregation. When mapping these flows, identify which steps must be synchronous and which can be deferred. For example, the redirect must synchronously read the mapping and perform a redirect, but recording a click count can be queued to an event stream. Common pitfalls include making analytics synchronous, which can increase redirect latency, or accepting custom codes without a namespace strategy, which risks collisions under heavy write rates. Write the flows as numbered steps, annotate sync versus async, and use that to determine caching and database read patterns. URL Shortener Use Cases and Flows means identify which operations must complete immediately and which can be deferred; this informs caching, queues, and database choices.. In practical terms, shorten, redirect, and optional management operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Use Cases & Flows
Primary Flow (synchronous)

Shorten → Return → Redirect

  1. Client submits a long URL to the shorten API; server validates input and generates a unique short code.
  2. Server stores mapping and returns the short URL. Storage must be durable enough that subsequent redirects succeed.
  3. When a short URL is requested, the service resolves the code and issues an HTTP redirect to the original URL with low latency.
Note: the shorten API should commit the mapping before responding for immediate availability; the redirect path must be optimized for read performance.
Optional & Async Flows
Custom codes
Require collision detection and namespace rules; may need to check an index or shard for uniqueness.
Analytics (async)
Emit click events to a queue to aggregate later. Keep analytics off the critical redirect path to preserve latency.
Expiration / Cleanup
Schedule background jobs to expire and delete mappings or mark them inactive without blocking redirects.
Common mistake: making analytics synchronous or not planning for custom-code collisions at scale.

screens.title: Pastebin Use Cases and Flows
screens.narratorSegment: A Pastebin service centers on two core operations: create a new paste and retrieve an existing paste. When a user creates a paste they provide content; the system must store that content and return a unique identifier or URL. Retrieval must deliver the stored content for viewing, applying any syntax highlighting or access control rules. Optional features include paste expiration, password protection, syntax highlighting, and account management. Unlike redirects, some paste features such as syntax highlighting affect presentation and can be applied at read time or pre-processed at write time depending on performance trade-offs. Access control adds complexity: private or password-protected pastes require authentication checks on each retrieval, which affects latency and caching strategy. A common misconception is to cache private pastes aggressively; correct design respects access controls and caches only public content or caches encrypted blobs with proper keying. For storage planning, pay attention to the variability in paste sizes — while many are small, occasional large pastes require chunking, quotas, or archive policies to avoid unbounded growth. Pastebin Use Cases and Flows means paste size variability and access controls influence storage, caching, and processing choices more than the simple create/retrieve functions.. In practical terms, create, retrieve, and access control patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Pastebin Flows
Core Flow

Create → Store → Retrieve

  1. User submits text content; server validates and assigns an ID or URL.
  2. Server stores the content durably and returns the paste URL immediately for access.
  3. Visitor requests paste URL; server enforces access control and renders the content, optionally with syntax highlighting.
Decide whether syntax highlighting is applied at write time or read time based on expected read frequency and latency goals.
Optional Concerns
Access control
Private or password-protected pastes require authentication on retrieval and careful caching rules.
Size variability
Average paste size is small, but large uploads require quotas, chunking, and storage tiering.
Expiration
Support for automatic expiry needs background cleanup and retention policy management.
Why it matters: misjudging paste sizes or caching private content can lead to performance and security issues.

screens.title: URL Shortener vs Pastebin: Workload Characteristics
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing the two systems clarifies design direction. A URL Shortener is typically read-heavy: many more redirects than creations. The chapter's assumptions show this clearly: 100 million new short URLs per month but an average of 10 clicks per URL leads to roughly 1 billion redirects per month. That means redirects dominate infrastructure needs, so the design should optimize for read throughput, caching, and very low latency. In contrast, a Pastebin has fewer writes and reads in the provided assumptions: 10 million pastes per month with about five views each, which yields a much lower RPS and a stronger emphasis on storage planning because paste sizes vary. Storage is also different: URL entries are compact and predictable, while paste content can range from a byte to megabytes, requiring quota and tiering policies. Operational focus shifts accordingly: for shorteners prioritize caching, replication for availability, and collision avoidance; for a paste service prioritize durable storage, access control, and handling variable object sizes. Recognizing these differences guides database choice, CDN use, and caching strategies. URL Shortener vs Pastebin: Workload Characteristics means read-heavy systems need aggressive caching and low-latency stores; variable-size storage requires quotas and tiering.. In practical terms, compare reads, writes, storage, and operational focus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Comparison
URL Shortener
Primary load: Read-heavy redirects (high RPS)
Data size: Small, fixed-size records per mapping
Operational focus: low-latency lookups, caching, collision avoidance
Design implication: use a highly available, low-latency read path with CDN or in-memory caches for hot codes.
Pastebin
Primary load: Balanced, lower RPS than shorteners in provided assumptions
Data size: Variable; many small pastes and some large ones
Operational focus: durable storage, access control, quota management
Design implication: plan for storage tiering and quotas; cache only public, frequently accessed pastes.

screens.title: Estimating Capacity for a URL Shortener
screens.narratorSegment: Capacity estimation converts user numbers into infrastructure requirements. Using the chapter's assumptions for the URL Shortener — 100 million new short URLs per month and 10 clicks per URL — we compute writes and reads per second. Divide 100 million by the number of seconds in a month to get roughly 38.5 writes per second; rounding up for peaks and uneven traffic, plan for about 50 WPS. For reads: 100 million URLs times 10 clicks equals 1 billion redirects per month, which becomes about 385 RPS on average; round up for peaks and plan for 500 to 1000 RPS to be safe. For storage, the chapter estimates ~300 bytes per entry leading to ~30 GB per month and about 1.8 TB over five years. Those numbers drive decisions: how many cache nodes, how large the database cluster, and whether to use a CDN. A common mistake is to use average rather than peak numbers when sizing caches and connection pools. Always document assumptions and include a safety multiplier for bursts and growth. Estimating Capacity for a URL Shortener means use averages for baseline and multiply for peaks; document assumptions and safety factors.. In practical terms, from monthly totals to wps, rps, and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Capacity Estimation
Calculations (visual)
100,000,000 new URLs / month
Seconds/month ≈ 30 * 24 * 3600 = 2,592,000
WPS ≈ 100,000,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 38.5 → plan for 50 WPS (peaks)

Reads: assume 10 clicks per URL
1,000,000,000 redirects / month
RPS ≈ 1,000,000,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 385 → plan for 500-1000 RPS

Storage per entry ≈ 300 bytes
100,000,000 * 300 bytes = 30 GB / month → ~1.8 TB over 5 years
Use these numbers to size caches, database shards, and connection pooling. Record your assumptions in every design discussion.
Implications & Notes
  • Plan for read-heavy scaling: CDNs and in-memory caches reduce load on the primary store.
  • Keep redirect path minimal: avoid synchronous analytics on the critical path.
  • Document peak factors and growth assumptions for capacity planning and cost estimates.
Remember: averages are a starting point; design for reasonable multipliers to handle bursts.

screens.title: Estimating Capacity for a Pastebin
screens.narratorSegment: Applying the chapter's paste assumptions, we compute baseline loads and storage. Ten million new pastes per month corresponds to about 3.8 writes per second; rounding for peaks we plan for 10 WPS. Assuming an average of five views per paste gives fifty million views per month, which is roughly 19 RPS on average; again round up and plan for 50–100 RPS to handle bursts. Storage is the trickiest part because paste size varies. The chapter assumes an average paste size of 5 KB, so ten million pastes yield about 50 GB per month and roughly 3 TB over five years. But real systems see heavy-tailed distributions: a few large pastes can dominate storage. That implies quotas, upload limits, chunked storage, and tiering to cheaper archival storage for infrequently accessed large items. Design your ingestion path to enforce size limits or to detect large uploads and route them to an object store. These controls keep operational costs and backups predictable. Estimating Capacity for a Pastebin means average paste size helps estimate storage, but quotas and tiering are essential to control cost and performance when sizes vary widely.. In practical terms, writes, reads, and the importance of handling variable sizes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

10,000,000 new pastes / month
Seconds/month ≈ 2,592,000
WPS ≈ 10,000,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 3.86 → plan for 10 WPS (peaks)

Assume 5 views per paste
50,000,000 views / month

Average paste size ≈ 5 KB

screens.title: Key NFRs: Availability, Latency, Durability, and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements specify how well the system performs its functions. For both services the chapter highlights a common set: high availability, low latency, scalability, durability, consistency, and security. High availability means the service remains usable even when components fail — this drives redundancy and regional failover. Availability

Low Latency

Durability

Decide which operations need immediate visibility and which can be eventual to gain performance.

screens.title: Common Challenges and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Designing these services surfaces recurring trade-offs. Consistency versus availability is a central one: ensuring that a newly created short URL is immediately readable pushes for synchronous writes and strong consistency, but that can increase latency or reduce availability during failures. A practical compromise is to make the core mapping commit synchronous while allowing analytics to be eventually consistent. Collision avoidance for short codes is another challenge. Approaches include deterministic hash-based generation with a collision resolution strategy, using a centralized ID generator, or partitioned namespaces for custom codes. Each option trades complexity, latency, and operational simplicity. Abuse prevention matters for both services: rate limiting, quotas, content scanning, and moderation pipelines help protect resources and legal compliance. A common operational mistake is to focus on average behavior and forget to provision for spikes and the long tail of large uploads or viral redirects. Document assumptions, pick realistic safety multipliers, and plan monitoring and alerting for sudden traffic patterns. screens.title: Common Interview Questions and the 'Paste Not Found' Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Two assessment ideas in the chapter help reinforce learning. First, a high-traffic social platform prioritizes the redirect service's NFRs: high availability and low latency are most critical because users expect instant link navigation. This is the correct interview answer when click volumes are enormous. Second, the Pastebin "Paste Not Found" then later works scenario is a classic signal of consistency issues: a write was not visible to a subsequent read immediately. In distributed systems this often results from eventual consistency on replicas or caches. A likely cause is that the paste was written to one replica while a read hit another replica that had not yet received the update. The fix depends on requirements: if immediate read-after-write visibility is required, enforce strong consistency on the write path or route reads to the primary until replication completes. If eventual consistency is acceptable, document the behavior and ensure clients can retry. In interviews, explain trade-offs and how you would instrument to detect and measure such inconsistencies. Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Assessment & Troubleshooting
Interview question
Which NFR is most critical for a high-traffic redirect service? The chapter answer is: high availability and low latency. Explain why: billions of redirects require always-on service with sub-second responses; sacrificing availability here harms user experience immediately.
Practice explaining trade-offs: if you favor availability, you may accept eventual consistency for analytics or click counts to avoid slowing redirects.
Troubleshooting scenario
User creates a paste, gets a URL, then immediately sees "Paste Not Found" but it works seconds later. Cause: consistency lag between replicas or caching layers. Fixes: synchronously commit and route reads to the primary for a short period, or surface eventual consistency to clients and encourage retry logic.
Assessment tip: always state assumptions, show calculations, and describe instrumentation to validate your design (metrics for replication lag, cache hit/miss rates, and error rates).

fullNarratorScript:
Before designing any system, we must stop and understand what the system must do and how it must behave. In this chapter you will learn how to list functional requirements, translate quality needs into non-functional requirements, and produce initial capacity estimates that feed architecture choices. We study two small but instructive systems: a URL Shortener, which converts long links into short ones and must redirect extremely quickly, and a Pastebin, which stores text snippets for retrieval. You will see concrete use cases for creating, retrieving and managing content, and learn why redirects are read-heavy while pastes can be more balanced. We will also cover common trade-offs: availability vs consistency, latency vs cost, and durability strategies for stored content. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write clear requirement statements, perform QPS and storage calculations using the supplied assumptions, and identify the top operational risks to plan for. Think of this chapter as the foundation: if requirements and capacity are wrong, every later architectural decision becomes brittle. As you move forward, ask yourself which NFRs matter most to your users and how that changes storage, caching, and replication choices.

In this first objectives slide, we set clear, testable skills you should gain. Objective one asks you to identify and separate functional requirements from non-functional requirements for both a URL Shortener and a Pastebin. You will learn to write concise functional statements like "shorten a given URL" or "create a new paste", and then pair each with the relevant quality constraints such as latency, availability, or security. Objective two focuses on capacity estimation: you will practice turning monthly or yearly volumes into writes per second, reads per second, and storage needs using the chapter's assumptions. This is not arithmetic practice alone — it's the habit of converting user stories into infrastructure requirements. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic that helps you remember whether an item is a function or a quality attribute, and a milestone marker you can use to verify competency. By practicing these objectives you will avoid a common mistake: designing systems before quantifying load and quality targets.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying and validating the skills you practiced earlier. You will practice calculating peaks and buffers: for example, rounding average writes and reads up to account for bursts and growth. The goal is to learn to design with a safety margin — we recommend planning for two to five times expected average RPS for peak capacity. You will also learn to reason about storage growth over years, not just months, and how that affects backup and retention choices. Finally, you will learn to translate user stories into acceptance criteria: e. g., a newly created short URL must redirect within a second, or a paste must be retrievable immediately after creation. Each card contains a mnemonic and a small micro-check you can use to confirm you have achieved the milestone. These are practical skills you will use in interview scenarios and real designs, where assumptions must be explained and justified.

A functional requirement states what the system must do. For a URL Shortener the core must-have functions are simple and specific: first, shorten a given URL — accept a long URL and return a unique short code or short URL; second, redirect a short URL to the original long URL. Those two requirements drive the A P I surface and the minimum data model: a short code, the original URL, creation metadata, and optional expiration or owner fields. Optional functional features often asked for in interviews include custom short codes, URL expiration rules, analytics for click counts and referrers, and user accounts for management. Each optional function adds complexity: custom codes require collision checks and namespaces, expirations add lifecycle management and cleanup jobs, and analytics need event collection and aggregation. A common misconception is to treat analytics as a core requirement; in many designs it can be implemented asynchronously to avoid slowing redirects. As a takeaway, write each function as a one-line statement and annotate whether it must be synchronous, can be eventual, or is optional. That clarity helps later decisions about consistency and performance.

Understanding the user flows makes it easy to convert requirements into APIs and operations. The primary flow for a URL Shortener has three steps: client submits a long URL, the system returns a short URL or code, and later a client requests the short URL which triggers a redirect to the original. Optional flows add steps: a user may request a custom code which requires collision checks, or set an expiration that schedules deletion. Analytics introduces a write-heavy event pipeline: each redirect can emit a click event with metadata for later aggregation. When mapping these flows, identify which steps must be synchronous and which can be deferred. For example, the redirect must synchronously read the mapping and perform a redirect, but recording a click count can be queued to an event stream. Common pitfalls include making analytics synchronous, which can increase redirect latency, or accepting custom codes without a namespace strategy, which risks collisions under heavy write rates. Write the flows as numbered steps, annotate sync versus async, and use that to determine caching and database read patterns. URL Shortener Use Cases and Flows means identify which operations must complete immediately and which can be deferred; this informs caching, queues, and database choices.. In practical terms, shorten, redirect, and optional management operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Pastebin service centers on two core operations: create a new paste and retrieve an existing paste. When a user creates a paste they provide content; the system must store that content and return a unique identifier or URL. Retrieval must deliver the stored content for viewing, applying any syntax highlighting or access control rules. Optional features include paste expiration, password protection, syntax highlighting, and account management. Unlike redirects, some paste features such as syntax highlighting affect presentation and can be applied at read time or pre-processed at write time depending on performance trade-offs. Access control adds complexity: private or password-protected pastes require authentication checks on each retrieval, which affects latency and caching strategy. A common misconception is to cache private pastes aggressively; correct design respects access controls and caches only public content or caches encrypted blobs with proper keying. For storage planning, pay attention to the variability in paste sizes — while many are small, occasional large pastes require chunking, quotas, or archive policies to avoid unbounded growth. Pastebin Use Cases and Flows means paste size variability and access controls influence storage, caching, and processing choices more than the simple create/retrieve functions.. In practical terms, create, retrieve, and access control patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing the two systems clarifies design direction. A URL Shortener is typically read-heavy: many more redirects than creations. The chapter's assumptions show this clearly: 100 million new short URLs per month but an average of 10 clicks per URL leads to roughly 1 billion redirects per month. That means redirects dominate infrastructure needs, so the design should optimize for read throughput, caching, and very low latency. In contrast, a Pastebin has fewer writes and reads in the provided assumptions: 10 million pastes per month with about five views each, which yields a much lower RPS and a stronger emphasis on storage planning because paste sizes vary. Storage is also different: URL entries are compact and predictable, while paste content can range from a byte to megabytes, requiring quota and tiering policies. Operational focus shifts accordingly: for shorteners prioritize caching, replication for availability, and collision avoidance; for a paste service prioritize durable storage, access control, and handling variable object sizes. Recognizing these differences guides database choice, CDN use, and caching strategies. URL Shortener vs Pastebin: Workload Characteristics means read-heavy systems need aggressive caching and low-latency stores; variable-size storage requires quotas and tiering.. In practical terms, compare reads, writes, storage, and operational focus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Capacity estimation converts user numbers into infrastructure requirements. Using the chapter's assumptions for the URL Shortener — 100 million new short URLs per month and 10 clicks per URL — we compute writes and reads per second. Divide 100 million by the number of seconds in a month to get roughly 38.5 writes per second; rounding up for peaks and uneven traffic, plan for about 50 WPS. For reads: 100 million URLs times 10 clicks equals 1 billion redirects per month, which becomes about 385 RPS on average; round up for peaks and plan for 500 to 1000 RPS to be safe. For storage, the chapter estimates ~300 bytes per entry leading to ~30 GB per month and about 1.8 TB over five years. Those numbers drive decisions: how many cache nodes, how large the database cluster, and whether to use a CDN. A common mistake is to use average rather than peak numbers when sizing caches and connection pools. Always document assumptions and include a safety multiplier for bursts and growth. Estimating Capacity for a URL Shortener means use averages for baseline and multiply for peaks; document assumptions and safety factors.. In practical terms, from monthly totals to wps, rps, and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Applying the chapter's paste assumptions, we compute baseline loads and storage. Ten million new pastes per month corresponds to about 3.8 writes per second; rounding for peaks we plan for 10 WPS. Assuming an average of five views per paste gives fifty million views per month, which is roughly 19 RPS on average; again round up and plan for 50–100 RPS to handle bursts. Storage is the trickiest part because paste size varies. The chapter assumes an average paste size of 5 KB, so ten million pastes yield about 50 GB per month and roughly 3 TB over five years. Non-functional requirements specify how well the system performs its functions. For both services the chapter highlights a common set: high availability, low latency, scalability, durability, consistency, and security. High availability means the service remains usable even when components fail — this drives redundancy and regional failover. Low latency, especially for redirects, pushes us toward in-memory caches, CDNs, and minimal request paths. Durability ensures that once a URL is shortened or a paste is saved, the data is not lost, which implies backups and replication strategies. Consistency is about visibility of writes: the chapter notes that immediate availability is desirable for short URLs and pastes, but some secondary features like analytics can be eventual. Security is critical for Pastebin because user content can include scripts; protect against XSS and implement proper content sanitization and access controls. Designing these services surfaces recurring trade-offs. Consistency versus availability is a central one: ensuring that a newly created short URL is immediately readable pushes for synchronous writes and strong consistency, but that can increase latency or reduce availability during failures. A practical compromise is to make the core mapping commit synchronous while allowing analytics to be eventually consistent. Collision avoidance for short codes is another challenge. Approaches include deterministic hash-based generation with a collision resolution strategy, using a centralized ID generator, or partitioned namespaces for custom codes. Each option trades complexity, latency, and operational simplicity. Abuse prevention matters for both services: rate limiting, quotas, content scanning, and moderation pipelines help protect resources and legal compliance. A common operational mistake is to focus on average behavior and forget to provision for spikes and the long tail of large uploads or viral redirects. Document assumptions, pick realistic safety multipliers, and plan monitoring and alerting for sudden traffic patterns.
